questions.name: Weather
questions.keyword: METAR wind direction speed decode
questions.text: A remote pilot is reviewing a METAR report before a commercial sUAS flight. The report contains the group '27015KT.' What information does this group convey?

answers.text: Wind from 015 degrees (north-northeast) at 270 knots, indicating an extreme weather event
Wind from 270 degrees (west) at 15 knots, with no gusts reported
Visibility of 270 statute miles with a ceiling at 15,000 ft MSL
Temperature of 27 degrees Celsius with a dew point of 15 degrees Celsius

explanations.a: The first three digits are always the wind direction and the next two digits are the speed; 015 and 270 are transposed in this interpretation.
explanations.b: In a METAR, the wind group is formatted as direction in degrees true followed by speed and units; '27015KT' means wind from 270 degrees (west) at 15 knots.
explanations.c: Visibility and ceiling are separate METAR groups decoded differently; the wind group beginning with three direction digits followed by speed digits does not encode visibility or ceiling.
explanations.d: Temperature/dew point is a separate METAR group, typically formatted as 'TT/TdTd' near the end of the report; the wind group always precedes visibility.

questions.name: Weather
questions.keyword: METAR ceiling layer BKN OVC decode
questions.text: The sky condition portion of a METAR reads 'FEW015 BKN040 OVC080.' A remote pilot needs to determine the ceiling for flight planning purposes. What is the ceiling, and which sky coverage type defines it?

answers.text: OVC080 defines the ceiling at 8,000 ft AGL because overcast layers always take precedence over broken and few layers
BKN040 defines the ceiling at 4,000 ft AGL because the ceiling is the lowest broken or overcast layer
FEW015 defines the ceiling at 1,500 ft AGL because it is the lowest reported cloud layer
No ceiling exists because at least one FEW layer is present, indicating overall sky conditions are predominantly clear

explanations.a: The ceiling is defined by the lowest BKN or OVC layer, not automatically by the highest overcast layer; BKN040 is lower than OVC080 and therefore sets the ceiling.
explanations.b: In aviation meteorology, the ceiling is defined as the height above ground of the lowest broken (BKN) or overcast (OVC) cloud layer; with BKN040 and OVC080 both present, BKN040 at 4,000 ft AGL is the ceiling.
explanations.c: FEW coverage (1/8 to 2/8) does not constitute a ceiling; the ceiling is defined by the lowest broken (BKN, 5/8 to 7/8) or overcast (OVC, 8/8) layer.
explanations.d: FEW layers do not establish or negate a ceiling; the presence of BKN040 defines the ceiling at 4,000 ft AGL regardless of the FEW layer below.

questions.name: Weather
questions.keyword: METAR visibility statute miles 3SM minimum VFR
questions.text: A remote pilot reviews a METAR that shows '3SM' in the visibility group. Under 14 CFR Part 107, what is the minimum flight visibility required to operate an sUAS, and does the observed 3 SM satisfy that requirement?

answers.text: The minimum visibility is 3 statute miles; the observed 3 SM exactly meets the regulatory minimum for Part 107 sUAS operations
Part 107 imposes no visibility minimum; the remote pilot may fly in any observed visibility as long as VLOS is maintained
The minimum visibility is 5 statute miles; 3 SM falls below this and the operation cannot proceed without a waiver
The minimum visibility is 1 statute mile; 3 SM exceeds this, so the flight is authorized under Part 107

explanations.a: Under 14 CFR 107.51(c), the minimum flight visibility for sUAS operations is 3 statute miles; an observed visibility of 3 SM exactly meets this regulatory minimum.
explanations.b: Part 107 does explicitly impose a visibility minimum of 3 statute miles; the regulation is 14 CFR 107.51(c) and the remote pilot may not operate in conditions below this threshold.
explanations.c: 5 statute miles is the VFR minimum for Class B, C, D, and surface Class E airspace for manned aircraft; the Part 107 sUAS minimum is 3 statute miles.
explanations.d: The Part 107 minimum visibility is 3 statute miles, not 1 statute mile; 3 SM meets the minimum exactly but does not exceed it.

questions.name: Weather
questions.keyword: TAF validity period terminal aerodrome forecast
questions.text: A remote pilot is planning an sUAS operation at a location served by a Terminal Aerodrome Forecast (TAF). The TAF is listed as valid from 1200Z to 1200Z the following day. How long is a standard TAF valid, and what geographic area does it cover?

answers.text: A TAF is valid for 6 hours and covers a 10-mile radius around the airport for which it is issued
A TAF is valid for 48 hours and covers weather conditions for all airports within a 50-mile radius of the issuing station
A TAF is valid for 24 hours (or 30 hours for major airports) and covers a 5-statute-mile radius around the issuing airport
A TAF is valid for 12 hours and covers the entire terminal control area (TCA) surrounding the primary airport

explanations.a: Standard TAFs are valid for 24 hours, not 6 hours; the coverage radius is 5 statute miles from the issuing airport.
explanations.b: TAFs cover 5 statute miles around the issuing airport, not 50 miles; the 48-hour validity period is not standard for TAFs.
explanations.c: A standard TAF is valid for 24 hours from the time of issuance, with some major airports issuing 30-hour TAFs; the forecast covers conditions within approximately 5 statute miles of the center of the airport.
explanations.d: TAFs are valid for 24 hours (or 30 hours at select stations), not 12 hours; TCA is an obsolete term not used in current TAF context.

questions.name: Weather
questions.objective: 5.1 Aviation weather sources — ASOS AWOS identification
questions.keyword: AWOS ASOS automated weather observation differences
questions.text: A remote pilot approaches weather briefing and must choose between ASOS and AWOS data for a flight near a small general aviation airport. What is the primary operational distinction between an ASOS and an AWOS station?

answers.text: ASOS is operated by the FAA exclusively at large commercial airports, while AWOS is used only by the military at air bases
ASOS and AWOS provide identical data sets; the distinction is purely administrative and has no operational significance for pilots
AWOS provides forecasts while ASOS provides only current observations; pilots should always use AWOS for planning and ASOS for pre-takeoff checks

ASOS (Automated Surface Observing System) is a joint NWS/FAA/DOD system providing more comprehensive data including precipitation type, while AWOS (Automated Weather Observing System) is FAA-operated with fewer sensor suites

explanations.a: ASOS is a joint program among NWS, FAA, and DOD and is not limited to large commercial airports; AWOS is not a military-only system.
explanations.b: ASOS and AWOS differ in their sensor capabilities, operating agencies, and data comprehensiveness; these differences have practical significance for pilots evaluating weather data quality.
explanations.c: Neither ASOS nor AWOS produces weather forecasts; both provide current automated surface observations; TAFs and area forecasts are the forecasting products.
explanations.d: ASOS is a National Weather Service, FAA, and DOD joint program that provides more comprehensive weather observations including precipitation identification, while AWOS is an FAA system with various levels of sensor capability; both provide automated weather data but ASOS generally has more complete sensor suites.

questions.name: Weather
questions.keyword: surface analysis chart isobar pressure system identification
questions.text: A remote pilot reviews a surface analysis chart and notices closely spaced isobars forming a pattern labeled 'L.' What does this pattern indicate, and how should a remote pilot interpret it for operational planning?

answers.text: Closely spaced isobars labeled 'L' indicate a high-pressure system with light, stable winds; ideal conditions for sUAS operations
Closely spaced isobars with 'L' indicate a calm center surrounded by moderate peripheral winds; sUAS operations should focus on the center of the 'L'
The 'L' label and closely spaced isobars indicate a stationary front with no wind movement; sUAS operations should be delayed until the front passes
The pattern indicates a low-pressure system; closely spaced isobars around an 'L' indicate strong pressure gradients and potentially strong, turbulent winds

explanations.a: An 'L' on a surface analysis chart denotes a low-pressure center, not a high-pressure system; high pressure is marked 'H' and is typically associated with fair weather and stable conditions.
explanations.b: Low-pressure centers do not have calm centers with moderate peripheral winds for favorable operations; the center of a low is associated with converging, rising air and unsettled weather.
explanations.c: A stationary front is depicted as an alternating red/blue line with triangles and semicircles on opposite sides; the 'L' label indicates a low-pressure center, not a stationary front.
explanations.d: On surface analysis charts, 'L' marks a low-pressure center; closely spaced isobars indicate a steep pressure gradient, which is associated with strong winds; low-pressure systems also bring unstable air, clouds, and precipitation, making conditions less favorable for sUAS operations.

questions.name: Weather
questions.objective: 5.3 Weather phenomena — density altitude effect on sUAS performance
questions.keyword: density altitude high elevation hot day performance degradation
questions.text: A remote pilot plans an sUAS agricultural survey in a high-elevation valley during a hot summer afternoon. The field elevation is 5,500 ft MSL, the outside temperature is 38°C (100°F), and humidity is high. The pilot notices the sUAS seems sluggish during hover. What meteorological condition best explains this performance reduction?

answers.text: The high humidity increases air mass weight, producing more lift than expected and reducing control responsiveness
High pressure associated with clear summer days at altitude compresses rotor downwash, reducing the effective thrust of the propellers
The extreme temperature heats the motor electronics, causing a thermal shutdown that limits available power to 60% of rated capacity
The high elevation combined with high temperature and humidity creates a high density altitude, reducing air density and degrading propeller efficiency and lift

explanations.a: High humidity actually reduces air density (water vapor is lighter than dry air), which decreases lift rather than increasing it; the premise is physically incorrect.
explanations.b: High pressure is associated with clear days but produces lower density altitude (denser air), not reduced performance; it is low pressure and high temperature that elevate density altitude.
explanations.c: While motor thermal limits can affect performance, the described sluggishness across all flight conditions is more consistent with reduced air density from high density altitude than a localized thermal shutdown.
explanations.d: Density altitude combines pressure altitude with temperature and humidity effects; at high elevation with high temperature and humidity, density altitude is significantly higher than field elevation, meaning the air is less dense, propellers produce less thrust for a given RPM, and the sUAS experiences degraded performance.

questions.name: Weather
questions.objective: 5.3 Weather phenomena — wind effect on sUAS
questions.keyword: wind gust sUAS operational limit control challenge
questions.text: A remote pilot arrives at the launch site and observes winds at 12 knots with gusts to 24 knots. No manufacturer-specific wind limits are available for the sUAS being used. Under Part 107 performance considerations, how should the pilot factor in gusts during this flight planning decision?

answers.text: Only the sustained wind speed of 12 knots matters; gusts are transient and do not affect the remote pilot's go/no-go decision
The average of sustained wind and gust value (18 knots) is the standard planning figure used under FAA guidelines for sUAS operations
Flights are automatically prohibited when gusts exceed sustained wind speed by more than 10 knots per Part 107 operating limitations
The pilot should use the gust factor (24 knots) as the effective maximum wind speed for planning purposes, since gusts represent the peak instantaneous load on the sUAS structure and control system

explanations.a: Gusts represent sudden, sharp increases in wind speed that can exceed the sUAS control system's ability to maintain stability; dismissing gusts in planning is hazardous.
explanations.b: Averaging sustained wind and gusts is not the FAA-recommended or standard approach; the peak gust value governs the most challenging condition the aircraft will face.
explanations.c: Part 107 does not establish a specific numerical gust-to-sustained-wind difference prohibition; operational judgment based on aircraft capability and preflight familiarization is the applicable standard.
explanations.d: When wind gusts are present, the gust value represents the peak wind speed the aircraft will actually experience; remote pilots should evaluate the sUAS's ability to handle peak gust loads, not just the sustained wind, because gusts impose the most severe structural and control demands.

questions.name: Weather
questions.keyword: cloud clearance 500 below 1000 above 2000 horizontal
questions.text: A remote pilot plans to fly at 350 ft AGL in Class G airspace. A scattered cloud layer sits at approximately 800 ft AGL. Under 14 CFR Part 107, what minimum cloud clearance distances must the remote pilot maintain?

answers.text: Maintain 500 feet below the cloud and 2,000 feet horizontally; the manned-aircraft rule of '1,000 above' does not apply to Part 107 sUAS
500 feet below and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds, per 14 CFR 107.51(c)
Same as VFR cloud clearance for manned aircraft: 500 below, 1,000 above, and 2,000 feet horizontally in Class G
1,000 feet below and 1 statute mile horizontally, applying the Class B above-10,000-ft VFR rule to Part 107

explanations.a: This is correct in substance, but option (b) states the rule itself; (b) is the precise Part 107 minimum.
explanations.b: Under 14 CFR §107.51(c), Part 107 cloud clearance is 500 feet below the cloud and 2,000 feet horizontal. There is no above-cloud minimum because Part 107 sUAS operate well below typical ceilings.
explanations.c: The '500 below / 1,000 above / 2,000 horizontal' rule is the 14 CFR §91.155 minimum for manned-aircraft VFR in some airspace classes; it does not apply to Part 107 sUAS operations.
explanations.d: Part 107 does not impose Class B's above-10,000-ft VFR cloud-clearance minimums on sUAS; the §107.51(c) rule applies regardless of airspace class.

questions.name: Weather
questions.keyword: thunderstorm development cumulus mature dissipating stages
questions.text: A remote pilot observes a large cumulus cloud building rapidly over the operation area during a planned afternoon sUAS flight. Understanding thunderstorm development, which statement best describes when a thunderstorm becomes most hazardous and what characteristics indicate that stage?

answers.text: The dissipating stage is the most hazardous because rainfall is heaviest and lightning frequency reaches its maximum during cloud breakdown
The mature stage is the most hazardous, characterized by simultaneous updrafts and downdrafts, heavy precipitation, lightning, and possible hail and wind shear
The cumulus stage is the most hazardous because updrafts are at their strongest and the cloud is still growing vertically
All three thunderstorm stages present equal hazard to aircraft; the safest policy is to avoid all cumulonimbus clouds regardless of stage

explanations.a: The dissipating stage is characterized by downdrafts taking over and precipitation decreasing; lightning can still occur but the most intense hazards including updraft/downdraft turbulence and hail peak in the mature stage.
explanations.b: The mature stage of a thunderstorm is characterized by both updrafts and downdrafts occurring simultaneously, creating extreme turbulence; heavy precipitation including hail, maximum lightning frequency, wind shear, and potential microbursts make the mature stage the most hazardous to aircraft.
explanations.c: The cumulus stage features primarily updrafts and is dangerous, but it has not yet produced the full range of hazards; the mature stage is considered most hazardous overall.
explanations.d: While avoiding all cumulonimbus clouds is correct practice, the stages are not equally hazardous; understanding the mature stage as most dangerous informs better decision-making about the urgency of avoidance.

questions.name: Weather
questions.keyword: thunderstorm lightning strike avoidance distance sUAS
questions.text: During a late afternoon sUAS mapping mission, a remote pilot observes a rapidly developing cumulonimbus cloud approximately 5 miles away. Thunder is audible. The pilot considers continuing because the cloud is currently upwind. What is the correct action under sound aeronautical decision-making?

answers.text: Continue the mission at reduced altitude because lightning typically strikes only in the precipitation core directly beneath the cloud
Continue only if VLOS is maintained and the cloud does not visibly approach the sUAS operating area within the next 10 minutes
Immediately terminate the flight and shelter the crew; audible thunder means the storm is within approximately 10 miles and lightning can strike well ahead of visible precipitation
Reduce flight altitude to 50 ft AGL and fly directly away from the cloud at maximum speed to increase the safe separation distance

explanations.a: Lightning can and does strike well outside the precipitation core, including in clear air ahead of the storm; reducing altitude does not adequately mitigate lightning risk.
explanations.b: Continuing while monitoring the cloud does not account for the fact that thunderstorms can rapidly intensify and move; audible thunder means the storm is close enough to pose an immediate hazard.
explanations.c: If thunder is audible, the storm is within approximately 10 miles; lightning can strike 10 miles or more from the cloud, well ahead of visible precipitation; the safe action is to immediately terminate the sUAS flight and shelter personnel — 'When thunder roars, go indoors.'
explanations.d: Flying at 50 ft AGL at maximum speed does not eliminate lightning risk and may introduce additional hazards from low-altitude obstacles; landing and sheltering is the correct action.

questions.name: Weather
questions.objective: 5.6 Fog types — radiation fog versus advection fog
questions.keyword: radiation fog calm clear night ground cooling
questions.text: A remote pilot arrives at a sunrise flight location and finds dense fog in the valley. The sky was clear overnight with calm winds and high relative humidity was reported. What type of fog is most likely responsible for these conditions, and when can the pilot expect it to dissipate?

answers.text: Advection fog moved in from a nearby water body and will persist until the wind direction changes to push it back offshore
Upslope fog formed as moist air moved up the valley walls and will dissipate only when surface temperatures drop below the dew point
Radiation fog formed from radiative cooling of the ground on a clear, calm night; it typically dissipates a few hours after sunrise as solar heating warms the surface
Precipitation fog formed from rain falling through dry air below a frontal system; it will lift when the associated frontal system passes the area

explanations.a: Advection fog forms when warm, moist air moves horizontally over a cooler surface; the conditions described (calm winds, clear sky, high humidity) are classic radiation fog conditions, not advection fog.
explanations.b: Upslope fog forms as air is mechanically lifted along terrain slopes; a valley calm-night situation with clear sky describes radiation fog, not upslope fog.
explanations.c: Radiation fog forms on calm, clear nights when the ground radiates heat rapidly, cooling the near-surface air to its dew point; it is most common in valleys and low-lying areas and typically burns off within a few hours of sunrise as solar heating increases surface temperature.
explanations.d: Precipitation fog (sometimes called steam fog) is a different phenomenon; the described conditions with clear overnight skies and calm winds point to radiation fog, not precipitation-induced fog.

questions.name: Weather
questions.keyword: advection fog coastal warm moist air cool surface
questions.text: A remote pilot operating near the Pacific coast notices that dense fog rolls in from the ocean during the afternoon despite relatively warm daytime temperatures. This fog persists through the day and does not dissipate with solar heating as expected. Which fog type best fits this description, and why does solar heating fail to dissipate it?

answers.text: Radiation fog; solar heating fails to dissipate it because the cloud layer above traps solar radiation and prevents surface warming
Frontal fog; the fog is associated with a stationary front whose cold air mass prevents solar heating from reaching the surface fog layer
Upslope fog; terrain channeling focuses the fog against the coast and solar heating is absorbed by the terrain rather than the air mass
Advection fog; it is continuously replenished by the ongoing horizontal flow of warm, moist marine air over the cool coastal surface, counteracting solar heating

explanations.a: Radiation fog forms overnight and typically dissipates after sunrise; its persistence through afternoon under warm conditions is not characteristic of radiation fog.
explanations.b: Frontal fog can be persistent but is associated with a moving or stationary front and frontal precipitation; the described coastal marine scenario is classic advection fog.
explanations.c: Upslope fog is driven by air being lifted along terrain; coastal afternoon persistence driven by ongoing marine flow is characteristic of advection fog, not upslope fog.
explanations.d: Advection fog forms when warm, moist marine air moves horizontally over a cooler ocean current or coastal surface; because the moist marine air flow is continuous, solar heating at the surface does not permanently dissipate the fog — new fog is constantly being formed by the ongoing air mass movement over the cool surface.

questions.name: Weather
questions.keyword: temperature inversion traps pollutants restricts vertical mixing
questions.text: A remote pilot notices that early morning visibility is reduced and smoke from a nearby industrial facility lies in a flat horizontal layer at approximately 200 ft AGL rather than dispersing vertically. What atmospheric condition is responsible for this phenomenon?

answers.text: A frontal passage where the leading edge of a cold front acts as a physical barrier preventing smoke from rising above 200 ft AGL
A strong surface high-pressure system producing downburst winds that physically push smoke horizontally across the terrain
A temperature inversion, where a warm air layer aloft traps cooler, denser air near the surface and prevents upward mixing of smoke and pollutants
A thermal layer caused by intense solar heating that creates a rotor zone at 200 ft AGL, circulating smoke in a confined horizontal band

explanations.a: Cold fronts cause rapid mixing and lifting of air, which would disperse smoke; they do not create a physical barrier that holds smoke flat at a specific altitude.
explanations.b: High-pressure downbursts would mix air vertically and disperse smoke, not trap it in a flat horizontal layer; high pressure is associated with subsidence inversions but the mechanism is not downburst winds.
explanations.c: A temperature inversion occurs when temperature increases with altitude rather than decreasing normally; the warm air aloft acts as a cap, preventing cooler surface air and smoke from rising through the inversion layer, causing pollutants to concentrate near the surface.
explanations.d: Thermal activity produces rising columns of air (thermals) that would lift smoke vertically; thermal zones cause vertical, not horizontal, mixing of air masses.

questions.name: Weather
questions.keyword: unstable atmosphere cumulus development turbulence
questions.text: A remote pilot observes rapidly building cumulus clouds and reports of mechanical turbulence during an afternoon sUAS flight over a sun-heated dark parking lot. Which statement best describes the atmospheric condition present and its effect on sUAS operations?

answers.text: The atmosphere is stable; cumulus development indicates a temperature inversion that limits vertical air movement to the cloud base level
The atmosphere is conditionally unstable; only the air inside cumulus clouds is turbulent and the sUAS operating below cloud base is unaffected
The atmosphere is in a neutral state; cumulus clouds are always present in mid-latitude climates and have no practical effect on sUAS below 1,000 ft AGL
The atmosphere is unstable; differential heating of the surface generates thermals and mechanical turbulence that can significantly affect sUAS control

explanations.a: Rapidly building cumulus clouds indicate atmospheric instability, not stability; temperature inversions suppress convection rather than promote cumulus development.
explanations.b: Turbulence associated with an unstable atmosphere extends below cloud base; the rising and sinking air columns forming cumulus clouds originate at the surface and affect aircraft well below the cloud base.
explanations.c: Rapidly building cumulus clouds indicate active convection and an unstable atmosphere; the claim of no practical effect below 1,000 ft AGL is incorrect because the turbulent mixing occurs precisely in the lowest layers.
explanations.d: An unstable atmosphere, often driven by solar heating of varying surface types (dark pavement heats faster than vegetation), generates thermal updrafts and turbulence; sUAS flying in thermally active environments can experience sudden updrafts, downdrafts, and control challenges, particularly at low altitudes where mixing is most pronounced.

questions.name: Weather
questions.objective: 5.8 Pressure altitude and density altitude calculation
questions.keyword: pressure altitude altimeter setting standard 29.92 in Hg
questions.text: A remote pilot needs to calculate pressure altitude at an airport with a field elevation of 2,800 ft MSL and a current altimeter setting of 30.22 in. Hg. Using the standard approximation, what is the pressure altitude?

answers.text: Approximately 2,500 ft, calculated by subtracting the deviation from standard pressure (30.22 − 29.92 = 0.30 in., × 1,000 ft/in. = 300 ft reduction)
Approximately 3,100 ft, calculated by adding the deviation from standard pressure to the field elevation
Approximately 2,800 ft because field elevation and pressure altitude are always equal when the altimeter is set to local altimeter setting
Approximately 4,022 ft, calculated by adding the altimeter setting in hundredths to the field elevation directly

explanations.a: The standard approximation is: pressure altitude = field elevation + (29.92 − current altimeter setting) × 1,000; here (29.92 − 30.22) × 1,000 = −300, so pressure altitude = 2,800 − 300 = 2,500 ft; because actual pressure is higher than standard, pressure altitude is lower than field elevation.
explanations.b: Adding the deviation would incorrectly raise pressure altitude when actual pressure exceeds standard; the correct formula subtracts 1,000 ft for each inch above 29.92 in Hg.
explanations.c: Field elevation and pressure altitude are equal only when the altimeter setting is exactly 29.92 in Hg (standard atmosphere); any deviation from 29.92 creates a difference.
explanations.d: Adding the raw altimeter setting digits to field elevation does not produce pressure altitude; the calculation requires the deviation from standard (29.92) multiplied by approximately 1,000 ft per inch.

questions.name: Weather
questions.objective: 5.8 Pressure altitude and density altitude calculation
questions.keyword: density altitude high temperature performance loss hover ceiling
questions.text: On a hot day at a high-elevation airport, a remote pilot calculates a density altitude of 7,500 ft while the field elevation is only 4,200 ft MSL. What performance change should the remote pilot anticipate for the sUAS compared to operations at sea level on a standard day?

answers.text: Improved performance because the thinner air creates less aerodynamic drag on the propellers and airframe
Improved stability due to reduced air mass turbulence at high density altitude conditions
No significant performance change because sUAS electric motors produce constant thrust independent of air density
Significantly degraded performance including reduced thrust for a given RPM, longer time to reach hover, and reduced payload capacity

explanations.a: Reduced aerodynamic drag does occur at lower air density, but this benefit is more than offset by the loss of propeller efficiency and thrust; sUAS performance degrades at high density altitude.
explanations.b: High density altitude is associated with unstable, thermally active air, not improved stability; density altitude reduces performance and does not improve handling qualities.
explanations.c: Electric motors do produce consistent electrical power output, but propeller thrust depends on air density; at lower air density, the same motor RPM generates less thrust, directly degrading performance.
explanations.d: At high density altitude, air is less dense, so propellers must spin faster to generate the same thrust; battery consumption increases, flight times decrease, payload capacity is reduced, and hover ceilings may be exceeded more quickly — all resulting in significantly degraded performance.

questions.name: Weather
questions.keyword: microburst intense downdraft short duration gust front sUAS
questions.text: A remote pilot observes a virga (precipitation that evaporates before reaching the ground) falling from a cumulonimbus cloud nearby. Shortly afterward, a brief but violent wind gust sweeps across the operating area, followed by calm. What weather phenomenon likely produced this sequence of events?

answers.text: A cold front passage where the leading edge of advancing cold air displaces warm surface air, creating a temporary gust line
A sea breeze front collision with outflow from an offshore storm, generating the gust before the front continues inland
A squall line that passed through the area at high speed; squall lines typically last 3 to 5 minutes and are always preceded by virga
A microburst, where intense evaporative cooling from virga creates a strong downdraft that spreads outward upon hitting the surface, producing a brief but severe wind shift and gust

explanations.a: Cold front passages produce a sustained wind shift and temperature change over a period of minutes to hours, not a brief violent gust followed immediately by calm; they are not typically triggered by virga.
explanations.b: Sea breeze fronts occur over coastal areas and are not specifically triggered by virga or associated with the brief intense sequence described; microburst is the specific phenomenon matching the described virga-to-violent-gust-to-calm sequence.
explanations.c: Squall lines are multi-cell thunderstorm systems associated with sustained winds; they are not triggered by virga and do not last only 3 to 5 minutes.
explanations.d: Microbursts occur when precipitation or virga evaporates in dry air below a cumulonimbus cloud, causing intense evaporative cooling that creates a powerful column of descending air; upon reaching the surface this downdraft spreads outward in all directions, producing an intense, brief gust front lasting 2 to 5 minutes with winds potentially exceeding 100 knots; the calm that follows marks the end of the downdraft divergence.

questions.name: Weather
questions.objective: 5.9 Wind shear and mechanical turbulence near terrain
questions.keyword: mechanical turbulence downwind of obstacle lee eddy
questions.text: A remote pilot is planning an sUAS building inspection on the downwind (leeward) side of a large multistory structure during a 20-knot wind day. What hazardous condition should the remote pilot anticipate on the downwind side of the building?

answers.text: Smooth laminar airflow because the building blocks the wind entirely, creating an aerodynamic shadow with no turbulence
Reduced humidity and increased temperature from adiabatic warming as air descends the leeward wall of the building
Accelerated steady winds because the Venturi effect compresses airflow around the building corners, increasing speed on the leeward side
Mechanical turbulence and eddies caused by airflow separating and recirculating behind the obstacle, creating unpredictable gusts and direction changes

explanations.a: The downwind side of a large obstacle does not produce smooth laminar flow; airflow separation and recirculation create turbulent eddies, not an aerodynamic calm.
explanations.b: Adiabatic warming is a phenomenon associated with descending air over mountain ranges (the Foehn effect); it is not a significant factor in airflow around a multistory building.
explanations.c: The Venturi acceleration effect is most pronounced at the corners and sides of a building, not on the downwind side; the leeward face is dominated by turbulence, not accelerated laminar flow.
explanations.d: When airflow encounters a large obstacle such as a building, it separates from the surface and forms turbulent eddies and rotor zones on the leeward side; these eddies produce unpredictable gusts and rapid direction changes that are particularly hazardous for sUAS operating close to the structure during inspection flights.

questions.name: Weather
questions.objective: 5.1 Aviation weather sources — winds aloft forecast FA
questions.keyword: winds aloft forecast 9000 ft direction speed decode
questions.text: A remote pilot reviews a winds aloft forecast and reads the group '2318' for the 3,000-foot level. How should this winds aloft group be decoded?

answers.text: Wind from 230 degrees at 18 knots, no temperature data included at this altitude level
Wind from 023 degrees at 18 knots with a temperature of 23 degrees Fahrenheit
Wind from 230 degrees at 18 knots; above 24,000 ft the temperature is also encoded, but the 3,000-foot level omits it
Wind from 180 degrees at 23 knots; the group reverses direction and speed digits at lower forecast altitudes

explanations.a: In winds aloft forecast products, the four-digit group is decoded as: first two digits = wind direction in tens of degrees (23 = 230°), second two digits = wind speed in knots (18 = 18 kt); for levels at or below 24,000 ft, temperature is not appended to the group.
explanations.b: The first two digits represent direction in tens of degrees (23 = 230°, not 023°); the digits are not read as a direct degree value.
explanations.c: The decoding of direction as 230° and speed as 18 knots is correct, but the note about temperature at 24,000 ft is also relevant; however, the full statement in option A is the most accurate and complete answer for the 3,000 ft level.
explanations.d: Wind direction and speed digits are not reversed in winds aloft coding at lower altitudes; the format is consistent across all forecast levels.

questions.name: Weather
questions.keyword: embedded thunderstorm IFR conditions instrument flight risk
questions.text: A remote pilot is briefed that thunderstorms are embedded within a large stratiform cloud layer covering the planned operating area. The surface visibility is reduced to 2 miles in mist and cloud ceilings are at 500 ft AGL. Which combination of regulatory and safety concerns prevents this sUAS flight?

answers.text: Only the embedded thunderstorm hazard prevents the flight; low visibility and ceiling are acceptable under Part 107 if VLOS is maintained
Only the 2-mile visibility prevents the flight because Part 107 requires 3 SM minimum; the embedded thunderstorm is manageable with proper positioning

Both the 2 SM visibility (below the 3 SM Part 107 minimum) and the 500 ft AGL ceiling with inadequate cloud clearance (below the 500 ft below-cloud minimum) prevent the flight; embedded thunderstorms add a severe safety hazard
The flight is permitted because visibility of 2 miles and 500 ft ceiling are acceptable in Class G airspace under the relaxed weather minimums applicable to sUAS operations at night

explanations.a: Multiple regulatory violations exist, not just the thunderstorm hazard; the visibility of 2 SM falls below the 3 SM Part 107 minimum, and cloud clearance cannot be maintained at 500 ft AGL if clouds are at 500 ft AGL.
explanations.b: The embedded thunderstorm is not merely 'manageable'; it represents a severe safety hazard that would independently prevent the flight; furthermore, the ceiling issue is also a regulatory violation.
explanations.c: This scenario has multiple compounding problems: visibility of 2 SM is below the 3 SM Part 107 minimum under 107.51(c); a ceiling at 500 ft AGL means the sUAS cannot maintain the required 500 ft below-cloud clearance above 0 ft AGL without violating 107.51(d); and embedded thunderstorms create extreme hazard to the sUAS and ground personnel.
explanations.d: Part 107's 3 SM visibility and cloud clearance minimums apply in all airspace classes; there are no relaxed weather minimums for sUAS at night or in Class G — in fact, night operations require anti-collision lighting but retain the same weather minimums.

questions.name: Weather
questions.keyword: fronts cold warm occluded stationary chart symbols
questions.text: A remote pilot interpreting a surface analysis chart identifies a line with alternating blue triangles and red semicircles pointing in opposite directions, with neither set of symbols moving. What type of front does this depiction represent, and what weather is typically associated with it?

answers.text: A cold front moving rapidly eastward, associated with a narrow line of severe thunderstorms and rapid wind shifts
A warm front moving slowly northward, associated with widespread stratiform clouds, drizzle, and gradually improving visibility
A stationary front that is not moving significantly in either direction, often associated with prolonged cloudiness, precipitation, and reduced visibility over an extended period
An occluded front where cold and warm fronts have merged, associated with complex precipitation and rapidly changing wind direction at the surface

explanations.a: A cold front is depicted as a line with solid blue triangles pointing in the direction of movement; alternating symbols on opposite sides is the stationary front symbol.
explanations.b: A warm front is depicted as a line with solid red semicircles on the side toward which the front is moving; the described alternating symbol pattern indicates a stationary front.
explanations.c: A stationary front is depicted as alternating blue triangles and red semicircles pointing in opposite directions — blue triangles on the cooler air side, red semicircles on the warmer air side; because neither air mass is advancing, the front stays in approximately the same location and can produce prolonged precipitation and reduced visibility.
explanations.d: An occluded front is depicted as a line with alternating purple triangles and semicircles pointing in the same direction; the described symbol with opposing directions is a stationary front.

questions.name: Weather
questions.objective: 5.3 Weather phenomena — turbulence clear air thermal activity
questions.keyword: thermal activity afternoon unstable conditions sUAS planning
questions.text: A remote pilot schedules an precision aerial photography mission for 2:00 PM on a clear summer day over a mixed landscape of dark pavement and open fields. The client requests stable, smooth imagery. From a weather perspective, when during the day would conditions most likely be smoothest for this photography flight?

answers.text: Mid-afternoon (1:00 to 3:00 PM) when solar heating is at its peak, generating maximum lift to counteract turbulence
Any time of day because electric motor vibration, not atmospheric turbulence, is the primary cause of image blur in sUAS photography
Late afternoon (4:00 to 6:00 PM) when sea breeze fronts arrive and stabilize the air mass over inland surfaces
Early morning, shortly after sunrise, when solar heating has not yet generated significant thermal activity and the atmosphere is most stable

explanations.a: Mid-afternoon is typically the most turbulent period of a clear summer day due to maximum solar heating generating thermal activity; this is the worst time for smooth imaging flights.
explanations.b: While vibration isolation is important for image quality, atmospheric turbulence is a significant and real source of sUAS motion that affects image stability; scheduling during low-turbulence periods meaningfully improves imagery.
explanations.c: Sea breeze fronts can introduce wind shifts and turbulence along the boundary; late afternoon in many locations experiences increasing instability and wind rather than calmer conditions.
explanations.d: Early morning, shortly after sunrise, is typically the most stable time of day for sUAS operations because nocturnal cooling has suppressed thermal activity, winds are usually lightest, and solar heating has not yet developed significant convection; this is the preferred time for smooth aerial photography.

questions.name: Weather
questions.keyword: PIREP pilot report turbulence icing wind shear value
questions.text: A remote pilot notices the following PIREP (Pilot Report) in a weather briefing: 'UA /OV MCO /TM 1430 /FL035 /TP C172 /SK BKN030 /TA 12 /TB LGT.' Which element of this PIREP is most relevant to an sUAS operation planning to fly at 350 ft AGL in the area?

answers.text: The BKN030 sky condition indicating a broken cloud layer at 3,000 ft AGL, which provides information about the ceiling relevant to cloud clearance planning
The FL035 (3,500 ft MSL) altitude, which indicates the sUAS would be operating 3,150 feet below the PIREP altitude and can safely ignore all reported conditions
The TB LGT (light turbulence) report, which indicates that even at 3,500 ft MSL, turbulence was light; the lower sUAS altitude would have no turbulence at all
The TP C172 element indicating a Cessna 172 made the report; manned aircraft PIREPs are not applicable to sUAS operations and should be disregarded

explanations.a: The sky condition BKN030 in the PIREP indicates a broken cloud layer at 3,000 ft AGL in the vicinity of MCO (Orlando International); for an sUAS operating at 350 ft AGL, this means the ceiling is approximately 3,000 ft AGL and cloud clearance requirements can be evaluated — 350 ft AGL is well below the cloud base, providing adequate clearance.
explanations.b: Operating well below the PIREP altitude does not mean all conditions can be ignored; the sky condition reported gives important context about the ceiling, which directly affects sUAS cloud clearance compliance.
explanations.c: Turbulence can extend to lower altitudes and is not necessarily absent below the reporting altitude; surface heating and mechanical turbulence commonly affect the lower levels regardless of what is reported aloft.
explanations.d: PIREPs from manned aircraft are valuable weather data applicable to all aviation including sUAS; disregarding them because of the report aircraft type would deprive the remote pilot of useful weather information.

questions.name: Weather
questions.objective: 5.3 Weather phenomena — wind effect on sUAS
questions.keyword: crosswind tailwind headwind effect sUAS performance planning
questions.text: A remote pilot is setting up for a long linear corridor inspection flight. The wind is directly from the left (90 degrees to the planned flight path). How does a direct crosswind affect the sUAS during a straight-line inspection pass?

answers.text: A crosswind causes the sUAS to drift laterally off the planned track if no correction is applied; the remote pilot or autopilot must apply crab angle or lateral correction to maintain the intended flight path
A crosswind has no effect on sUAS operations because multirotor aircraft compensate automatically with GPS hold and require no pilot input
A crosswind accelerates the sUAS beyond its groundspeed limit because the wind adds to the forward thrust vector of the aircraft
A crosswind reduces the effective payload capacity by 25% because the wind applies lateral force on the payload, stressing mounting hardware

explanations.a: A direct crosswind pushes the sUAS laterally off its intended track; to maintain a straight flight path, the remote pilot or autonomous system must apply a correction angle (crab) into the wind, similar to how manned pilots correct for crosswinds to maintain a desired ground track.
explanations.b: While GPS-based autopilots apply wind correction automatically, relying on GPS hold without monitoring for drift is poor airmanship; crosswinds still affect sUAS flight paths and battery consumption.
explanations.c: A crosswind is perpendicular to the flight path and does not add to forward speed; only a tailwind component adds to groundspeed.
explanations.d: Lateral aerodynamic force on payload mounting hardware is not the standard concern with crosswinds; the primary effect is drift off the intended flight path.

questions.name: Weather
questions.objective: 5.6 Fog types — steam fog over water
questions.keyword: steam fog cold air over warm water Arctic sea smoke
questions.text: A remote pilot plans an early morning sUAS water survey over a lake. Overnight temperatures dropped to near freezing while the lake water remained relatively warm. Upon arrival, the pilot observes wisps of fog rising from the lake surface into the cold air above. What type of fog is forming and should the remote pilot be concerned about flying in it?

answers.text: Radiation fog forming above the lake; it poses no hazard because it dissipates immediately when disturbed by rotor downwash
Upslope fog forming as lake air is pushed up the shoreline bank; it is harmless and poses no operational concern

Steam fog (Arctic sea smoke) forming as cold air moves over the warmer water surface; while typically shallow, it can reduce visibility near the surface and the pilot should assess actual VLOS conditions before operating
Precipitation fog from overnight rain evaporating at the lake surface; it always dissipates within 30 minutes of sunrise and poses no operational concern

explanations.a: Radiation fog forms from ground cooling, not from warm water evaporating into cold air; the described phenomenon is steam fog (evaporation fog).
explanations.b: Upslope fog forms from mechanical lifting of air along terrain; rising wisps from a warmer water surface into cold air is steam fog, not upslope fog.
explanations.c: Steam fog (also called Arctic sea smoke) forms when very cold air moves over a relatively warm water surface; evaporation from the water condenses in the cold air, creating rising wisps or patches of fog; while typically shallow, it can reduce surface visibility enough to impair VLOS and the remote pilot should assess whether actual visibility conditions allow safe operation.
explanations.d: Precipitation fog forms from rain falling through a dry air layer below a frontal system; the described condition of overnight freezing temperatures and warm water producing rising wisps is steam fog, not precipitation fog.

questions.name: Weather
questions.keyword: isobar spacing wind speed estimate surface analysis
questions.text: A remote pilot examines a surface analysis chart and observes that isobars are spaced closely together in one quadrant and widely spaced in another. How does isobar spacing relate to expected wind conditions in each area?

answers.text: Closely spaced isobars indicate light winds because the air molecules are packed tightly together and move slowly; wide spacing indicates stronger winds with more open flow
Isobar spacing has no relationship to wind speed; wind is driven exclusively by temperature differences between air masses, not pressure gradient
Closely spaced isobars indicate a steep pressure gradient and stronger winds; widely spaced isobars indicate a weak pressure gradient and lighter winds
Closely spaced isobars indicate high-pressure systems with calm conditions; widely spaced isobars always indicate low-pressure systems with stormy weather

explanations.a: Closely spaced isobars indicate a steep pressure gradient (large pressure change over a short distance), which drives stronger winds, not lighter winds; this is the opposite of the correct relationship.
explanations.b: The pressure gradient force is a primary driver of wind; pressure differences between adjacent areas are directly related to wind speed, making isobar spacing a useful wind speed indicator.
explanations.c: On a surface analysis chart, isobars connect points of equal pressure; closely spaced isobars indicate a steep pressure gradient (rapid pressure change with distance), which produces stronger winds; widely spaced isobars indicate a weak gradient and lighter winds.
explanations.d: The spacing of isobars does not by itself indicate whether a system is a high or low; isobar spacing indicates wind speed potential, and both high- and low-pressure systems can have closely or widely spaced isobars depending on the system's intensity.

questions.name: Weather
questions.objective: 5.3 Weather phenomena — precipitation types effect on sUAS
questions.keyword: freezing rain ice accumulation sUAS propeller airframe hazard
questions.text: A remote pilot receives a weather briefing warning of freezing drizzle in the planned operating area. The temperature at the surface is -1°C (30°F). The planned sUAS does not have any ice protection systems. Under aeronautical decision-making principles, should the remote pilot conduct the flight?

answers.text: Yes, because freezing drizzle is a light precipitation type that affects only manned aircraft with large wing surfaces; rotors are too small to accumulate significant ice
Yes, if the operation is limited to 5 minutes or less because ice accumulation on rotors requires sustained exposure to develop to a dangerous thickness
No, because ice accumulation on propellers changes blade geometry, disrupts airflow, and reduces lift and thrust; without ice protection the sUAS should not be flown in freezing precipitation
No, but only if the ambient temperature drops below -10°C; freezing drizzle above -10°C does not accumulate enough ice to affect rotor performance

explanations.a: sUAS rotors are very susceptible to ice accumulation; even small amounts of ice change the blade profile, reduce lift and thrust, and can cause vibration or catastrophic failure; the claim that rotors are too small to accumulate significant ice is incorrect.
explanations.b: Ice can begin accumulating on unprotected rotors almost immediately in freezing precipitation; a 5-minute limit is not a recognized operational standard and provides a false sense of safety.
explanations.c: Freezing precipitation deposits ice on all exposed surfaces including rotor blades; even thin ice accumulation changes blade geometry, reduces lift coefficient, increases drag, adds weight, and can cause vibration leading to structural failure; without anti-icing protection, sUAS should not be operated in any freezing precipitation.
explanations.d: Ice accretion begins at temperatures at or below 0°C when supercooled liquid water contacts surfaces; there is no -10°C threshold below which freezing drizzle becomes safe for unprotected rotors.

questions.name: Weather
questions.objective: 5.1 Aviation weather sources — aviation weather products overview
questions.keyword: graphical forecast for aviation GFA NWS web tool
questions.text: A remote pilot is planning a flight and wants to get a comprehensive graphical overview of current and forecast weather conditions including clouds, precipitation, and flight categories for the contiguous U.S. Which aviation weather product provides this information?

answers.text: The Graphical Forecast for Aviation (GFA), a web-based tool from the National Weather Service that provides interactive maps of current and forecast weather
The Transcribed Weather Broadcast (TWEB), which provides automated audio weather information available through VOR receivers tuned to specific frequencies
The Aircraft Communications Addressing and Reporting System (ACARS), which provides real-time weather uplinks to aircraft cockpit displays
The Collaborative Convective Forecast Product (CCFP), which is available exclusively to airline dispatchers and cannot be accessed by general aviation pilots

explanations.a: The Graphical Forecast for Aviation (GFA) at aviationweather.gov provides an interactive graphical interface showing current and forecast cloud cover, precipitation, icing, turbulence, wind, and flight categories (VFR/MVFR/IFR/LIFR) for the contiguous U.S. and is freely accessible to all pilots including remote pilots.
explanations.b: The TWEB was an older product that has been discontinued; it is no longer a current aviation weather resource for remote pilots.
explanations.c: ACARS is an aircraft-based data communications system used by commercial aircraft to receive weather and operational data; it is not a ground-based planning tool accessible to remote pilots.
explanations.d: The CCFP is a convective forecast product but it is available through aviationweather.gov; however, it is a specific convective planning tool and not the comprehensive graphical overview described in the question.

questions.name: Weather
questions.objective: 5.7 Atmospheric stability and pressure altitude effects
questions.keyword: high pressure system stability fair weather anticyclone
questions.text: A remote pilot checks the surface analysis chart and identifies a well-developed high-pressure system centered over the planned operating area. The high-pressure center shows 'H' with widely spaced isobars. What weather conditions should the pilot generally expect?

answers.text: Generally fair weather with stable air, light winds, good visibility, and limited cloud development due to subsiding air in the high-pressure center
Strong, gusty winds with rapidly changing direction as the anticyclone circulation accelerates air outward in all directions
Frequent afternoon thunderstorms as the high-pressure system heats the air mass and drives rapid convection throughout the day
Dense fog and low ceilings as the high-pressure system traps moisture at the surface and prevents evaporation

explanations.a: High-pressure systems (anticyclones) are characterized by subsiding air that warms adiabatically as it descends, suppressing cloud formation and thunderstorm development; they generally produce fair weather, light winds, and good visibility — ideal conditions for sUAS operations.
explanations.b: High-pressure systems are associated with light winds and descending air; they do not produce strong gusty outflow — that description better fits areas around active low-pressure systems.
explanations.c: High-pressure systems suppress convection through subsiding air; they are associated with fair weather, not afternoon thunderstorms; thunderstorms are associated with low-pressure systems and atmospheric instability.
explanations.d: While radiation fog can form within a high-pressure system at night under certain conditions, the general association of high pressure is with fair weather and good visibility, not persistent dense fog and low ceilings.

questions.name: Weather
questions.keyword: hail thunderstorm sUAS structural damage above freezing level
questions.text: A remote pilot observes a mature thunderstorm 8 miles away and notes the anvil-shaped top extending downwind at high altitude. Even though the sUAS is operating at only 300 ft AGL, the pilot should be concerned about which specific thunderstorm hazard that can affect aircraft well outside the visible precipitation area?

answers.text: Sonic booms from the supercell's rotating wall cloud, which can cause structural damage to sUAS frames at distances up to 10 miles
Hail falling outside the visible rain shaft, which can exit the storm's anvil at significant distance from the thunderstorm and fall through clear air
EMP pulses from the lightning strikes that can disable sUAS electronic systems within a 20-mile radius of the cell
Ground-level ozone produced by the lightning that increases air density and degrades sUAS propeller efficiency near the storm

explanations.a: Sonic booms are not produced by thunderstorms at the distances described; this is not a recognized thunderstorm hazard to aircraft.
explanations.b: Hail can be ejected from the thunderstorm updraft and carried downwind by upper-level winds in the anvil; it can then fall through clear air well outside the visible precipitation area, posing a hazard to aircraft including sUAS that are not beneath the visible storm.
explanations.c: EMP pulses capable of disabling avionics at 20-mile ranges are not a recognized thunderstorm phenomenon; while lightning does produce electromagnetic effects, a 20-mile disability radius for electronics is not supported by aviation weather science.
explanations.d: Ground-level ozone from lightning is not a recognized aviation hazard affecting air density or propeller performance; this is not a standard thunderstorm hazard cited in aviation meteorology.

questions.name: Weather
questions.objective: 5.9 Wind shear and turbulence near obstructions
questions.keyword: rotor turbulence lee side mountain ridge hazardous terrain
questions.text: A remote pilot is planning an sUAS survey flight over a ridgeline. The winds are blowing at 35 knots perpendicular to the ridge. The pilot knows that mountain wave turbulence and rotor zones can form on the lee side of ridges in these conditions. What hazard should the remote pilot primarily be concerned about when operating on the downwind side of the ridge?

answers.text: Reduced wind speed on the lee side that could cause the sUAS to lose translational lift and enter vortex ring state if hovering above the ridgeline
Rotor zone turbulence with severe and unpredictable vertical currents that can exceed the sUAS control authority and cause loss of control
Increased visibility due to dust being blown clear of the lee side; this is operationally beneficial but can lead to overconfidence in clear conditions
Positive pressure buildup on the lee slope that can push the sUAS into the terrain at high speed if the throttle is reduced

explanations.a: Translational lift and vortex ring state are hover-specific phenomena unrelated to mountain wave turbulence; the primary concern on the lee side in high winds is mechanical turbulence and rotor zones.
explanations.b: On the lee side of a ridge in strong winds, rotor zones can form where airflow separates and recirculates; these areas produce severe, unpredictable vertical currents (both updrafts and downdrafts) that can exceed the control authority of an sUAS, leading to loss of control or structural failure.
explanations.c: Dust clearance on the lee side is not the primary concern; severe turbulence is the dominant hazard.
explanations.d: Positive pressure buildup is a windward-side phenomenon; the lee side experiences low pressure and turbulent recirculating air, not a positive pressure force pushing aircraft into terrain.

questions.name: Weather
questions.objective: 5.1 Aviation weather sources — area forecast FA
questions.keyword: area forecast FA cloud tops weather hazards 18 hours
questions.text: A remote pilot requests a standard weather briefing and receives an Aviation Area Forecast (FA). What information does an Aviation Area Forecast typically provide, and how long is its forecast period?

answers.text: The FA provides real-time radar imagery and is continuously updated every 5 minutes by the National Weather Service radar network
The FA is a text forecast covering cloud heights, weather conditions, and hazards for a broad geographic area, valid for approximately 18 hours with a 12-hour outlook
The FA provides site-specific forecasts for individual airports within a defined region and is valid for exactly 24 hours with no extended outlook
The FA provides only surface wind forecasts at 1,000 ft AGL increments and is used exclusively for departure and arrival planning at major airports

explanations.a: The FA is a text-based forecast product, not a real-time radar product; radar imagery is provided through separate NWS and FAA tools such as the Aviation Weather Center radar displays.
explanations.b: The Aviation Area Forecast (FA) is a text-based weather forecast issued by NWS Aviation Weather Centers covering a broad geographic region; it includes cloud heights, turbulence, icing, and weather hazards, and is typically valid for 18 hours with an additional 12-hour outlook period.
explanations.c: The FA covers a broad geographic area, not individual airport sites; site-specific airport forecasts are covered by TAFs; the FA validity includes an 18-hour forecast period with a 12-hour outlook, not exactly 24 hours total.
explanations.d: Winds aloft forecasts (FB) provide wind and temperature forecasts at various altitude levels; the FA covers much broader weather conditions than just surface winds.

questions.name: Weather
questions.keyword: flight visibility in-flight measurement remote pilot obligation
questions.text: While conducting an sUAS mission, visibility conditions unexpectedly deteriorate. The remote pilot estimates visibility has dropped to approximately 2 statute miles due to increasing haze. Under 14 CFR Part 107, what action is required?

answers.text: Reduce sUAS altitude to below 100 ft AGL where haze is typically less dense and continue the operation at the lower altitude
Immediately terminate the flight because visibility has dropped below the 3 SM Part 107 minimum; the operation cannot legally continue
Continue for up to 15 minutes while contacting the nearest ASOS to obtain an official visibility reading, since estimated visibility is not sufficient to terminate a commercial flight
Activate the sUAS collision avoidance sensors, which can substitute for visual conditions when visibility falls below Part 107 minimums

explanations.a: Reduced altitude does not restore legal flight visibility; if ambient visibility is below 3 SM, the regulatory minimum is violated at all altitudes.
explanations.b: Under 14 CFR 107.51(c), the minimum flight visibility for Part 107 sUAS operations is 3 statute miles; if estimated visibility drops to 2 SM, the operation is below the regulatory minimum and must be terminated.
explanations.c: There is no 15-minute grace period for below-minimum visibility; commercial flight status does not extend weather minimum compliance windows; the flight must stop.
explanations.d: Collision avoidance sensors do not substitute for the Part 107 flight visibility minimum, which is based on the pilot's ability to see and avoid other aircraft and hazards; electronic sensors are supplemental, not regulatory replacements for weather minima.

questions.name: Weather
questions.keyword: convective SIGMET thunderstorm severe turbulence icing
questions.text: A remote pilot's preflight briefing includes a Convective SIGMET covering the planned operating area for the next 2 hours. A Convective SIGMET is issued for which specific weather conditions?

answers.text: Moderate or severe icing above 18,000 ft MSL, affecting commercial turbojet aircraft on transcontinental routes
Severe or extreme turbulence below 15,000 ft MSL in mountainous terrain caused by lee wave activity

Severe thunderstorms with surface winds over 50 knots or hail at the surface 3/4 inch or greater in diameter, or a tornado, or embedded thunderstorms, or lines of thunderstorms, or areas of thunderstorms covering at least 40% of an area
Moderate or greater turbulence and icing in any airspace regardless of storm activity, issued when surface winds exceed 25 knots at multiple reporting stations

explanations.a: Icing SIGMETs (AIRMETs SIERRA or SIGMETs for severe icing) address icing hazards; Convective SIGMETs are specifically about thunderstorm-related hazards, not icing above 18,000 ft.
explanations.b: Mountain wave turbulence SIGMETs and AIRMETs (TANGO) address severe mountain wave activity; Convective SIGMETs are issued for thunderstorm-specific hazards.
explanations.c: Convective SIGMETs are issued by the Aviation Weather Center for severe convective weather: severe thunderstorms with surface winds over 50 knots or surface hail 3/4 inch or more, tornadoes, embedded thunderstorms in clouds, lines of thunderstorms, or areas of thunderstorms covering 40% or more of a 3,000 square mile area.
explanations.d: General turbulence and icing are addressed by AIRMETs; Convective SIGMETs are specifically for thunderstorm hazards and are not triggered by surface wind thresholds at weather stations.

questions.name: Weather
questions.objective: 5.8 Pressure altitude and density altitude calculation
questions.keyword: dew point temperature spread fog likelihood relative humidity
questions.text: A remote pilot's preflight weather check shows a temperature of 18°C and a dew point of 16°C at the operating site. Based on this temperature-dew point spread, what should the remote pilot anticipate regarding fog or low visibility development if temperatures continue to fall overnight?

answers.text: Fog is unlikely because a 2-degree temperature-dew point spread indicates dry conditions with relative humidity well below the saturation threshold
Fog or low clouds are likely to form when the temperature drops to the dew point (16°C) as the air becomes saturated; the 2-degree spread indicates high relative humidity and proximity to saturation
Fog will form only if the wind speed exceeds 10 knots, which mechanically mixes the moist surface air with drier air aloft and accelerates saturation
The dew point is irrelevant to fog formation; fog develops exclusively from precipitation and cannot form from radiative cooling when skies are clear

explanations.a: A 2-degree temperature-dew point spread indicates high relative humidity (approximately 89%) and very close proximity to saturation; this small spread means fog is likely to form as temperatures drop overnight.
explanations.b: Fog forms when air cools to the dew point temperature and becomes saturated; a temperature-dew point spread of only 2°C indicates the air is already nearly saturated; continued cooling will bring the temperature down to the dew point (16°C), at which point fog or low clouds will likely develop — making this a significant planning concern for early-morning operations.
explanations.c: Fog actually forms more readily under calm winds; wind disperses surface cooling and fog formation requires relatively light or calm wind conditions.
explanations.d: Fog is a common product of radiative cooling on calm, clear nights when the surface cools rapidly and temperature drops to the dew point; precipitation is not required for fog formation.

questions.name: Weather
questions.objective: 5.3 Weather phenomena — relative wind translational lift sUAS
questions.keyword: translational lift airspeed effective ETL efficiency hover
questions.text: During an sUAS photography session requiring extended hovering over a subject, the remote pilot notices significantly higher battery consumption compared to previous forward-flight missions of similar duration. What aerodynamic principle explains why hovering is less efficient than forward flight for many multirotor sUAS?

answers.text: In hover, all thrust must overcome gravity with no translational lift component, requiring maximum motor output; forward flight introduces translational lift as undisturbed air enters the rotor disk, improving efficiency
Hovering causes the motors to overheat faster because the propellers create no airstream to cool the motor windings during stationary flight
In forward flight, battery voltage increases with airspeed because the relative wind acts as a generator through the motor windings, reducing net power draw
Hovering requires less power than forward flight because the aircraft has no aerodynamic drag in a stationary position; the higher consumption is due to payload weight, not the flight mode

explanations.a: In hover, the rotor recirculates already-disturbed air beneath the disk, requiring more power to generate the same thrust than in forward flight where the rotor encounters undisturbed (denser) incoming air; this phenomenon, related to translational lift in helicopter aerodynamics, means forward flight is generally more power-efficient than hover for multirotor aircraft.
explanations.b: While motor cooling can be relevant, the primary energy difference between hover and forward flight is the aerodynamic efficiency of the rotor system encountering undisturbed versus recirculated air, not motor temperature management.
explanations.c: The concept of a relative wind generating electricity through motor windings and reducing power draw is not a real aerodynamic or electrical phenomenon applicable to sUAS operations.
explanations.d: Hovering actually requires more power than efficient forward flight for the same weight; aerodynamic drag in forward flight is partly offset by the translational lift efficiency gain, making the statement about hover requiring less power incorrect.

questions.name: Weather
questions.objective: 5.9 Wind shear and turbulence near obstructions
questions.keyword: wake turbulence helicopter large aircraft avoidance sUAS
questions.text: A remote pilot is operating an sUAS at a general aviation airport with helicopter traffic. A large helicopter departs from a nearby helipad and passes 400 feet above the sUAS operating area. The remote pilot's crew member shouts a warning. What hazard is the sUAS at risk of encountering, and what is the correct response?

answers.text: Rotor downwash and vortex wake from the departing helicopter; the remote pilot should immediately maneuver the sUAS out of the helicopter's flight path and the area beneath and behind the helicopter's rotor wake
Engine exhaust heat from the turbine, which can damage sUAS electronics; the remote pilot should rotate the sUAS nose away from the exhaust direction and activate thermal protection mode

Electromagnetic interference from the helicopter's transponder, which can jam the sUAS control link; the pilot should switch to backup frequency and maintain hover until the helicopter's transponder clears the area
No significant hazard; FAA regulations require helicopters to fly at least 500 ft above all sUAS operating areas and the separation ensures safety without any pilot action needed

explanations.a: Helicopter rotor wash and wake vortices can extend well below and behind the rotor disk; an sUAS in this area can experience sudden uncontrolled movement, loss of control, or structural stress; the correct response is to immediately maneuver the sUAS away from the helicopter's path and the area beneath and downwind of the rotor wake.
explanations.b: Engine exhaust from a helicopter is not a standard hazard to sUAS electronics in the described scenario; the rotor downwash is the primary mechanical hazard.
explanations.c: Transponder electromagnetic interference is not a recognized cause of sUAS control link jamming in this context; rotor wash is the immediate physical hazard.
explanations.d: There is no FAA regulation requiring helicopters to maintain 500 ft separation from sUAS operating areas; helicopters operate at various altitudes including low-level transit, and remote pilots must yield to all manned aircraft and manage their proximity accordingly.

questions.name: Weather
questions.keyword: weather depiction chart flight categories VFR MVFR IFR LIFR
questions.text: A remote pilot reviews a Weather Depiction Chart and sees an area contoured with a hatched region labeled 'IFR.' What does the IFR designation indicate about expected conditions, and how does it affect sUAS operational planning?

answers.text: IFR conditions mean ceiling above 3,000 ft AGL and visibility above 5 SM; these are favorable conditions for all sUAS operations
IFR conditions indicate ceiling at or below 1,000 ft AGL and/or visibility at or below 3 SM; these conditions may violate Part 107 weather minimums and prevent safe sUAS operations
IFR conditions apply only to instrument-rated manned pilots and have no regulatory relevance to Part 107 sUAS operations in uncontrolled airspace
IFR conditions indicate moderate turbulence and wind shear; sUAS may operate in IFR conditions if the crew uses an onboard turbulence sensor to monitor gust intensity

explanations.a: IFR conditions are defined by low ceiling and/or visibility, not favorable high ceiling and visibility; the described conditions are VFR, not IFR.
explanations.b: Instrument Flight Rules (IFR) conditions are defined as ceilings at or below 1,000 ft AGL and/or visibility at or below 3 SM; these conditions are at or below Part 107's minimum flight visibility of 3 SM and may prevent maintaining required cloud clearances, making sUAS operations illegal or unsafe.
explanations.c: While IFR as a flight rule applies to manned aircraft, the weather conditions associated with IFR flight categories directly impact Part 107 weather minimums; a 3 SM visibility IFR condition exactly meets the Part 107 minimum, while below-minimum IFR prevents sUAS operations.
explanations.d: IFR is a weather-based flight category indicating low ceiling and/or visibility, not a turbulence category; turbulence is addressed separately through SIGMETs and AIRMETs, not IFR/VFR flight categories.
